title: Choosing a database
subtitle: Pick a database from how you read and write your data, not from what is popular. Then count what it costs to run.

c.v: Discord built the first version of its app in early 2015. Every chat message lived in one MongoDB
replica
set. This was on purpose, and the team planned a path to move later.
Around November 2015, they had 100 million stored messages. Then the data and the index no longer fit in RAM.
Latency
became unpredictable.

Before they picked a new database, they studied how the app really used messages. Reads were very random, and reads and writes were about 50/50. They also wrote down what they needed: linear scaling, automatic
failover
, low maintenance, predictable speed, a proven product, and open source.
Cassandra was the only database that met all of these needs. It also came with a trade-off. It gives up strong consistency to stay available. Discord wanted that, and accepted
eventual consistency
In 2017 the cluster had 12 Cassandra nodes. By early 2022 it had 177. Hot
partitions
compaction
backlogs and
garbage collection
pauses caused latency spikes.
In May 2022, Discord moved to 72 nodes of ScyllaDB, a Cassandra-compatible database. The
latency to read old messages fell from 40–125 ms to 15 ms.
So a choice is not "right forever". It fits a set of
access patterns
at one size. In this lesson you will learn to ask the questions Discord asked, before your data outgrows your database.
There is no best database. There are databases that fit some ways of reading and writing data, and fit others badly.
So start from your
access patterns
: which questions the app asks, how often, and how fast the answer must be. Then add your requirements:
transactions
, consistency, size, and who will run it at 3 a.m.
The key idea.
First list how you will read and write the data. Then pick the simplest database that serves those patterns, and that your team can run. Popularity is not a requirement.
DB-Engines sorts hundreds of systems by
data model
. Its main groups include relational, key-value, document, wide column, search engines, time series, graph and vector. Some systems belong to more than one group.
The AWS decision guide uses a similar list. It adds in-memory as a group and has no search engine group.
Step through the questions. Each "yes" points to a family. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
The main families, as their own docs describe them
Relational
(Postgres, MySQL). Tables,
joins
, constraints and
ACID
transactions. Postgres also stores JSON and supports every SQL
isolation level
Key-value
(DynamoDB, Redis). Get and put by key. AWS suggests it for session stores and shopping carts.
DynamoDB is fully managed and also has ACID transactions across tables.
Redis keeps data in memory.
Document
(MongoDB). JSON-like documents with nested fields, in collections without a fixed schema.
Wide-column
(Cassandra). Tables split into partitions across many nodes, with eventual consistency.
Search engine
(Elasticsearch). Built on Apache Lucene, it stores JSON documents in indices for search and analytics.
Time-series
(TimescaleDB, InfluxDB). TimescaleDB splits Postgres tables into chunks by time.
InfluxDB is built for event and time-series data, like server and sensor monitoring.
Graph
(Neo4j). Nodes and relationships. The links are stored with the data, so queries follow them without joins.
Vector
(pgvector). Finds the nearest vectors, for example similar texts. pgvector does this inside Postgres, next to your other data.
What each one is bad at
Each family pays for its strength somewhere.
Cassandra chose not to support transactions across partitions, distributed joins or
foreign keys
. Fast queries must give the
partition key
So you design one table per query, and changing the questions later is hard.
MongoDB has multi-document transactions. Its docs warn that a distributed transaction costs more than a single-document write, and that it does not replace a good schema.
Redis keeps data in memory (
Redis in depth
goes further). If you turn on its
append-only file
, the default policy syncs to disk once per second. A crash can then lose about 1 second of writes. With snapshots only, you can lose minutes.
That may be fine for a
cache
, but usually not for money.
Elasticsearch makes a new document searchable within about 1 second, not at once.
So keep the real data in your main database, and copy it into the search index.
Transactions and consistency
Ask: must several records change together, or not at all? Money, stock and bookings usually need this. Relational databases are built for it: Postgres has been ACID-compliant since 2001.
If you pick a store with weaker transactions, your app code must handle the gaps. The
transactions lesson
and the
CAP lesson
explain what you give up.
Scale
Write numbers, not adjectives. How many rows in two years? How many reads and writes per second at peak?

Kailash Nadh, the CTO of the Indian trading platform Zerodha, makes this point. A Postgres node with a replica, good partitions and indexes can hold hundreds of billions of records and terabytes of data.
He argues that you often do not need a distributed database.
This lesson agrees: most apps fit one Postgres for a long time. When they do not,
replication
and
sharding
come next.
Running cost and team skills
Someone must back it up, upgrade it, watch it and fix it at night. If you host it yourself, your team does the maintenance, monitoring and patching. A managed service takes most of that work.
It usually costs more per hour, so compare that with the engineer time it saves.
Skills matter too. AWS suggests that a team already running Postgres should first try pgvector before a new
vector store
Dan McKinley says a new technology brings more "unknown unknowns". He suggests a young company gets only a few "
innovation tokens
", maybe three, to spend on new tools.
Polyglot persistence
Using several stores in one system is called
polyglot persistence
. AWS gives a shop example: a
document store
for the catalogue, DynamoDB for fast browsing, and Aurora for orders and stock.
Martin Fowler wrote about it in 2011. He warns that it costs complexity. Each new store is a new interface to learn and to tune.
You also have to keep the copies in sync.
The table sums up the sources above. The "Bad at" column is partly this lesson's own advice, so test it against your own case.
Relational
Joins, constraints, ACID transactions, new queries later.
Writes beyond one big node need sharding.
Users, orders, payments. Most apps.
Key-value
Very fast get and put by key at huge scale.
Queries not by key need extra indexes. No joins.
Sessions, carts, cache.
Document
Nested records that match your code.
Data with many links between records. Multi-document transactions cost more.
Catalogues, profiles.
Wide-column
Heavy writes spread over many nodes.
Joins, cross-partition transactions, new query shapes.
Messages, events at very large scale.
Search engine
Ranked full-text search, typos, filters.
Being the main copy of the data. New data is not searchable at once.
Product and log search.
Time-series
Cheap writes and time-range queries.
Data that is not mostly timestamped points.
Metrics, sensors, prices.
Graph
Following many hops of links.
Simple lookups any database can do. One more system to run.
Fraud rings, recommendations.
Vector
"Find similar" by embedding.
Being the only store. You still need the source data.
Semantic search, RAG.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Write the access patterns first: the top 10 queries, read/write ratio, peak rate, and data size in two years.
Mark which data needs transactions. Money and stock usually do.
Start with the database the team already runs well. Ask "what can't it do?" and prove it with a test.
Prefer a feature of the current database (JSON column, pgvector, TimescaleDB) before a new system.
For each new store, name the owner, the backup plan, the
on-call
runbook
and the monthly cost.
Choose managed unless you have a clear reason and the people to self-host.
Plan how data gets into a second store, for example with
change data capture
, and how you rebuild it.
Write the decision down in a short record with the patterns, options, and the reason.
Checklist before you pick:
Access patterns listed?
Transactions needed where?
Size and rate in two years, as numbers?
Can the current database do it?
Who runs it, and is it managed?
How do you leave it later?

"Here are our 10 most common queries, our read/write ratio and our data size. For each database family, say which queries it serves well and which it serves badly. Do not recommend a product until the end."
"We run Postgres. We need vector search for 2 million documents. Compare pgvector with a separate vector store, including backups, sync and on-call work."
"List the operational tasks our team takes on if we self-host Cassandra instead of using a managed service. Link each task to the official docs."
The agent's family descriptions match the official docs, not a blog post or its memory.
Every claim like "scales to millions" names a source or comes from your own
load test
The comparison includes running cost: backups, upgrades, monitoring and on-call.
The answer says how data stays in sync between stores.
The agent did not pick the newest tool just because it is new.
Next:
Data modelling for NoSQL
shows how to design tables around access patterns. For how storage engines pay for writes, see
B-tree vs LSM-tree
. For search, see
Search and inverted indexes

q.v: You are starting a new shop app with users, orders and payments. Nobody has measured any load yet. What is the safest first choice?

options.v: A key-value store, so it can grow to any size.
One relational database such as Postgres.
Five different databases, one for each kind of data.

why.v: Orders and payments link to each other and need transactions. A relational database handles both, and you can add a store later for a proven need.

q.v: What made Discord leave its single MongoDB replica set?

options.v: MongoDB had no way to store text.
Around 100 million messages, the data and index no longer fit in RAM, and latency became unpredictable.

why.v: Discord's 2017 post says exactly this, around November 2015.

q.v: In Cassandra, which query is fast?

options.v: One that gives the partition key.

why.v: The Cassandra docs say all performant queries supply the partition key. Cross-partition transactions and distributed joins are not supported.

q.v: Your Postgres app needs "find similar products" with vector embeddings. What should you check first?

options.v: Whether the pgvector extension in your current Postgres is enough.
Which new vector database is the most popular this year.
Whether you can move all data to a graph database.

why.v: AWS suggests teams that already run Postgres start by trying pgvector. It keeps vectors next to the rest of the data.
